issues.legal_issue: A company for whose benefit land is acquired and which has an interest in the land or must pay the compensation is a person interested entitled to challenge a ruling in the acquisition proceeding.
material_facts: The land was acquired for the company's benefit under an agreement providing that it would be transferred to the company after vesting in the government.
Under the agreement, the company was responsible for paying the compensation.
The company appealed a ruling that it lacked standing because it was not a person interested.
issues.conclusion: The company was a person interested and could maintain its appeal; the High Court erred in dismissing the appeal for lack of locus standi.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 uses an inclusive definition of person interested, which must be construed liberally to include persons directly or indirectly interested in title to the land or the amount of compensation. The Court relied on Sunder Lal v. Paramsukhdas, The Hindustan Sanitaryware and Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana, Comilla Electric Supply Ltd. v. East Bengal Bank Ltd., and M. Kuppuswami v. The Special Tahsildar, and rejected the contrary view in State of Orissa v. Amarendra Pratap Singh and the contrary view attributed to the Calcutta High Court.

rule.if: land_acquired_for_company_benefit and (company_had_contractual_land_interest or company_bound_to_pay_compensation) and company_appealed_acquisition_ruling

predicates.land_acquired_for_company_benefit: The government acquired the land for the benefit of a company.
predicates.company_had_contractual_land_interest: An agreement provided that the land would be transferred to the company after it vested in the government.
predicates.company_bound_to_pay_compensation: An agreement made the company responsible for paying the compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.company_appealed_acquisition_ruling: The company appealed a ruling in the land acquisition proceeding.

issues.definition: When land is acquired for a company's benefit and the company has a contractual interest in the land or must pay the compensation, the company may challenge a ruling in the acquisition proceeding as a person interested.

issues.legal_issue: Retrospective validation of a company land acquisition requires completion of the acquisition through vesting of the entire acquired land in the government, and does not cure an acquisition that remains incomplete.
material_facts: The land had been acquired for a company before the retrospective validating amendment, and an award had been made.
The landowners and occupants remained in possession of the acquired land, and the government admitted that possession had not been fully taken.
Even assuming possession of part of the land had been taken, possession of the entire acquired land had not been transferred to the government.
The amendment was invoked to validate acquisition proceedings that had been held invalid.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was incomplete because the entire land had not vested in the government, so the amendment did not cure its invalidity; the acquisition proceedings remained void.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1962 could retrospectively validate a qualifying company acquisition made before the amendment, notwithstanding a prior court order, only if the acquisition was complete and the land had vested in the government. R. L. Arora v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1964) explains that vesting must occur under section 16 or section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; until possession of the entire acquired land is taken, the acquisition is not complete for this purpose.

predicates.company_acquisition_subject_to_retroacti: A party sought retrospective validation of an acquisition made for a company.
predicates.entire_acquired_land_possession_transfer: The government took possession of the entire land covered by the acquisition.

issues.definition: When retrospective validation is sought for a company acquisition but the government has not taken possession of the entire acquired land, the acquisition's invalidity is not cured.
